subject: Banking
title: Duration Risk and Bank Losses
description: A short lesson to help you apply Duration Risk and Bank Losses.

hook.text: Banks lend money for 30 years but take deposits that can leave tomorrow. This mismatch is called duration risk.

buildup.text: A bank issues a 30-year mortgage at 4%. If rates rise to 6%, that mortgage is now worth less than its face value.

discovery.text: Duration risk means banks hold assets that lose value when rates change. The longer the loan, the bigger the risk.

twist.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed because of duration risk. They held long-term bonds that lost $15 billion when rates rose.

climax.text: Lending long and borrowing short is how banks profit. It's also how they die when interest rates move against them.

punchline.text: Lend for 30 years, fund it daily. Duration risk is banking's core danger.

quiz.question: What is duration risk?
options: The mismatch between long-term loans and short-term deposits

details.summary: Duration risk is the danger that rising interest rates will cause long-term bonds to lose value. Banks holding large portfolios of low-rate bonds accumulated during the zero-rate era faced billions in unrealized losses when rates surged in 2022.
details.whyItMatters: Duration risk destroyed Silicon Valley Bank and threatened many others in 2023. Understanding it explains how a bank can appear profitable while sitting on massive hidden losses in its bond portfolio.
takeaways: Bonds lose value when interest rates rise; long-term bonds lose the most
US banks held over $600 billion in unrealized bond losses in 2023
Accounting rules allowed banks to hide these losses until bonds were sold

faq.question: How can a bank lose money on government bonds?
faq.answer: If a bank buys a 10-year Treasury paying 1.5% and rates rise to 4.5%, the market value of that bond drops roughly 25%. The bank gets full value at maturity, but if forced to sell early, it realizes a massive loss.

faq.question: Why did banks buy so many low-rate bonds?
faq.answer: During 2020-2021, banks were flooded with deposits from stimulus payments but loan demand was weak. They invested in government bonds for safe returns. When rates rose faster than anyone expected, these safe investments became the source of massive losses.
